title: Module 3 · Reading
desc: Analysing definitions, drawing inferences from scientific texts, and reading a research article critically.

topics.label: Part 1: Analysing Definitions
topics.summary: Types of definitions, the eight methods of expansion, and how to spot faulty definitions.

subtopics.label: 1.1 What Is a Definition?
subtopics.summary: A definition fixes a term's meaning, scope and boundaries; the type must suit purpose and audience.

subtopics.label: 1.2 Formal, Informal, Operational and Negative Definitions (*Analysing Definitions* deck)
subtopics.summary: Formal = term + class + distinguishing features; informal = plain words; operational = what is measured + threshold; negative = what it is not (weak alone).

subtopics.label: 1.3 Expanded Definitions: The Key Focus and Methods of Expanding Definitions
subtopics.summary: Extended definitions combine 2–4 expansion methods (function, structure, process, analogy, example, history, comparison, etymology).

subtopics.label: 1.4 Extended Definition Breakdown: Artificial Intelligence (Parts 1 and 2)
subtopics.summary: The AI example expands one simple definition through all eight methods, each answering a different question.

subtopics.label: 1.5 Exam Tips and Classroom Application
subtopics.summary: Score by opening formally, using 3–4 methods, avoiding circular wording and keeping the flow smooth.

subtopics.label: 1.6 The 8 Types of Definitions, and Lexical vs Stipulative (*Module 3* deck)
subtopics.summary: The Module 3 deck lists eight types (lexical, stipulative, operational, conceptual, extensional, synonym, ostensive, genus & difference).

subtopics.label: 1.7 Operational Definitions and Descriptive Definitions
subtopics.summary: Operational definitions make ideas measurable and repeatable; descriptive ones list observable features without prescribing.

subtopics.label: 1.8 Simple vs Extended Definitions, and Methods for Expanding a Definition (*Module 3* deck)
subtopics.summary: Simple definitions (class + characteristics) suit familiar readers; extended ones suit complex or contested concepts.

subtopics.label: 1.9 Definition Pitfalls: A Hall of Shame
subtopics.summary: Four faults: circular, too broad, too narrow, figurative only. Aim for one term, one clear meaning.

topics.label: Part 2: Reading Comprehension and Drawing Inferences
topics.summary: Surface vs deep reading, hedging, limitations and the four traps in research texts.

subtopics.label: 2.1 Surface Reading vs Deep Reading
subtopics.summary: Surface reading grasps the words; deep reading grasps what the text implies, assumes and avoids saying.

subtopics.label: 2.2 How to Draw Inferences Like a Pro
subtopics.summary: An inference is a reasoned conclusion from evidence: hunt hedges, read limitations, challenge the data, bring context.

subtopics.label: 2.3 Common Traps When Reading Research
subtopics.summary: Four traps: correlation as causation, cherry-picked data, jargon hiding weak claims, overgeneralisation.

topics.label: Part 3: The Research Article — Decoded
topics.summary: IMRaD and the article map, plus abstracts, introductions and reading order.

subtopics.label: 3.1 IMRaD: The Universal Language of Science
subtopics.summary: IMRaD: Introduction (problem), Methods (repeatable), Results (data only), Discussion (meaning).

subtopics.label: 3.2 Anatomy of a Research Article: The Full Map (Parts 1 and 2), with the Recap's Section Table
subtopics.summary: Full article map from title and abstract to references, each part with a distinct job.

subtopics.label: 3.3 How an Introduction Actually Works
subtopics.summary: Introductions make three moves: establish the territory, establish the niche (the gap), occupy the niche.

subtopics.label: 3.4 The Sixty-Second Abstract Test
subtopics.summary: An abstract answers what, why, how and so what, in order; vague methods are a warning sign.

subtopics.label: 3.5 Read in This Order, Not That One
subtopics.summary: Read abstract, conclusion, figures, methods first; introduction and discussion next; references last.

topics.label: Part 4: Analysing a Research Article
topics.summary: Critical-reading checklist, empirical vs humanities articles, and the annotate-and-return activity.

subtopics.label: 4.1 The Critical Reading Checklist
subtopics.summary: Six checks: specific question, fitting method, unspun results, discussion follows results, honest limitations, supported claims.

subtopics.label: 4.2 Not Every Article Is IMRaD
subtopics.summary: IMRaD is the empirical-science convention; humanities articles are thematic and may state the thesis late.

subtopics.label: 4.3 Activity: Read, Annotate, Return, and The One Thing to Remember
subtopics.summary: Five layered tasks on one article: label structure, define terms, draw inferences, separate claim from data, defend one sentence.

topics.label: Module 3 Worksheet A — CAT-2 Preparation (Open Book)
topics.summary: Open-book practice on two passages, definitions, article sections and abstract writing.

subtopics.label: Section A: Passage A — Reflective Roof Coatings in Informal Housing
subtopics.summary: Passage A (roof coatings): state findings, infer, spot what was not measured, compare hedged and overclaimed conclusions.

subtopics.label: Section B: Passage B — Evening Screen Use and Sleep Quality
subtopics.summary: Passage B (screen use and sleep): operational definition via PSQI, unclear direction, unreliable self-estimates, other factors.

subtopics.label: Section C: Working with Definitions
subtopics.summary: Sentence definitions with class and features, stipulative and operational definitions, fixing faults, expanding with three methods.

subtopics.label: Section D: Parts of a Research Article
subtopics.summary: Place extracts by wording, not topic: literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion.

subtopics.label: Section E: Putting It Together
subtopics.summary: Putting it together: write an abstract under 70 words and explain what a discussion or conclusion paragraph does that results do not.

title: Module 4 · Writing
desc: Review papers, the literature review, and APA / IEEE referencing.

topics.label: Review Papers & Literature Review
topics.summary: Five review types, how to tell them apart, and how to write a literature review.

subtopics.label: 5.1 What Even IS a Review Paper? and Anatomy of a Review Paper
subtopics.summary: A review synthesises existing research; skeleton runs from abstract to thematic body, discussion, conclusion and references.

subtopics.label: 5.2 The 5 Types of Reviews and Side-by-Side Showdown (with the Recap's Type Table)
subtopics.summary: Five review types (narrative, systematic, meta-analysis, scoping, critical) compared by scope, method and best use.

subtopics.label: 5.3 Type 1: Narrative Review and Type 2: Systematic Review
subtopics.summary: Narrative: broad, author-driven, biased risk. Systematic: strict reproducible protocol from identification to inclusion.

subtopics.label: 5.4 Type 3: Meta-Analysis and Type 4: Scoping Review
subtopics.summary: Meta-analysis pools comparable studies into a combined effect size; scoping maps how much research exists and the gaps.

subtopics.label: 5.5 Type 5: Critical Review
subtopics.summary: Critical reviews judge the quality and validity of literature; the point is judgement, not coverage.

subtopics.label: 5.6 The Literature Review: Your Research GPS and the 5-Step Formula
subtopics.summary: A literature review is a critical conversation: define scope, search, evaluate, synthesise by theme, write and cite in one style.

topics.label: Referencing
topics.summary: Why referencing matters; APA vs IEEE for journal articles and books.

subtopics.label: 5.7 Referencing: Why It's Not Optional, and the 5 Referencing Styles
subtopics.summary: Plagiarism costs marks and record; citation gives credit. Five styles exist: APA, IEEE, MLA, Chicago, Harvard.

subtopics.label: 5.8 APA vs IEEE, MLA/Chicago/Harvard, In-Text Citations, and Reference Lists vs Bibliographies
subtopics.summary: APA is author-date, IEEE numbered; a reference list holds cited sources, a bibliography all consulted.

subtopics.label: 5.9 Citation Cheat Sheet: One Example, Five Styles, and One Journal Article, Five Styles
subtopics.summary: One book and one article in five styles: only order, punctuation and italics change; never mix styles.

subtopics.label: 5.10 IEEE and APA, Rule by Rule, and Spot the Errors
subtopics.summary: Six APA/IEEE differences (author, year, title, journal, volume/issue, pages) and how to fix IEEE errors.

subtopics.label: 5.11 Name That Style, Common Citation Mistakes, and What CAT-2 May Ask You to Do
subtopics.summary: Recognise Harvard, MLA and Chicago by their giveaways; avoid mixed styles and uncited paraphrase.

title: CAT-2 · Recap
desc: Revision aids and the model CAT-2 paper, linked back to the notes.

topics.label: CAT-2 Recap & Model Paper
topics.summary: Exam-focused revision and the model CAT-2 paper.

subtopics.label: R1. What the Paper Looks Like and Before You Walk In
subtopics.summary: CAT-2 has five 10-mark questions; not examined: in-text citation, MLA, Chicago, Harvard; avoid summarising instead of inferring.

subtopics.label: R2. Model Paper Q1 — The Canteen Passage
subtopics.summary: Canteen passage: surface vs deep reading, hedging, the causation trap, limitations, weighed vs self-reported data.

subtopics.label: R3. Model Paper Q2 — Definitions (Drip Irrigation, Extract A)
subtopics.summary: Drip irrigation extract: formal, operational and informal definitions, then expansion methods.

subtopics.label: R4. Model Paper Q3 — Sections of a Research Article and the Abstract
subtopics.summary: Place five extracts by section with their job; write an abstract under 70 words answering four questions in order.

subtopics.label: R5. Model Paper Q4 — Types of Review
subtopics.summary: Identify scoping (counts, no quality check) vs systematic (registered protocol), justified by scope, method and best use.

subtopics.label: R6. Model Paper Q5 and Recap — APA and IEEE
subtopics.summary: APA and IEEE for one, two and three authors: pick or convert, watching &, "and", the comma, year position and pp.
